questions.enonce_markdown:
The World Wide Web is supported by a network infrastructure

(a) What is a computer network? (1 mark)

(b) Describe the tasks carried out by: a router and a web server. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Computer network (1 mark)**

A computer network is a collection of two or more computers and other devices (nodes) connected together by transmission media (cables or wireless links), so that they can communicate and share resources such as files, printers and an Internet connection.

**(b) Router and web server (4 marks)**

- **Router (2 marks).** A router connects two or more different networks (for example a school LAN and the Internet). For every packet it receives it reads the destination IP address, looks in its routing table to choose the best path (the next hop), and forwards the packet on the right interface. It therefore moves data between networks and keeps traffic from one network away from another; home routers also provide services such as NAT, DHCP and a firewall.
- **Web server (2 marks).** A web server is a computer running server software (for example Apache, Nginx or IIS) that stores web pages and their resources (HTML files, images, scripts). It listens for requests of browsers (clients) sent with the HTTP/HTTPS protocol, finds the requested page (or runs a server-side program, possibly querying a database, to build it), and sends the response back to the client. It can serve many clients at the same time and keeps logs and security controls.

questions.enonce_markdown:
EnohMakia is won a contract to network a university campus that has story buildings spread out in a large campus. The campus is situated in a geographical region where the is plenty of rainfall and thunder storms. Besides having a campus-wide network, each story buildings has to be networked, and computers must be locally connected if they are found within a given room (such as an office or teaching laboratory). EnohMakia can only network the university with one or more of twisted pair, coaxial and fiber optic cables.

(a) State which kind of cabling is best suited for each of campus-wide, story building and room networking justify your answer from properties associated with each network transmission medium. (6 marks)

(b) State and justify a network topology you would use to connect campus buildings. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Choice of cabling (6 marks)**

| Level | Best suited cable | Main reasons (properties) |
|---|---|---|
| Campus-wide (between buildings, outdoors) | **Fibre optic** | Carries light, not electricity: **immune to electromagnetic interference and to lightning-induced surges**, which matters in a region of thunder storms (copper cables running between buildings can pick up surges and damage equipment); very **high bandwidth**; very **low attenuation**, so runs of several kilometres without repeaters; **hard to tap** (secure); not corroded by rain. It is more expensive, but this is the backbone. |
| Story building (between floors and rooms inside a building) | **Coaxial cable** | Its braided screen gives **better protection from interference** than twisted pair; bandwidth higher than twisted pair; segments of a few hundred metres (about 185 m thin, 500 m thick) are enough for a building; **cheaper** than fibre and easier to install in ducts. |
| Room (computers in an office or laboratory) | **Twisted pair (UTP)** | **Cheap**, thin and **flexible**, very easy to install and to connect (RJ45 connectors) to a switch; bandwidth (100 Mbit/s to 1 Gbit/s) and length (up to 100 m) are enough for a room; interference is limited over short distances. |

(Fibre can also be accepted inside the building when high speed is required; the answer is marked on the quality of the justification from the properties of each medium.)

**(b) Topology to link the campus buildings (2 marks)**

A **star topology** (a star of stars, the "extended star"): the network of each building is connected, by fibre, to a central switch or router in the main building. Justification: each building has its own link, so a **cable fault affects only one building**; faults are **easy to locate** and a new building is **easy to add** without disturbing the others; the traffic is managed centrally. Its weakness is the central device, which is a single point of failure and can be duplicated. (A ring or a mesh with redundant links is also acceptable if justified by the greater reliability.)
